power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Consumer experiences and perceptions of change during psychotherapy for suicide imagery -a mixed-methods case series of Integrated skills for SUicide IMagery (I-SUIM)

author.affiliation:
Centre for Clinical Interventions 6
								Murdoch University

text.text: Background and objectives: This study is the first to explore mechanisms of change and engagement experiences for consumers completing a tailored intervention involving imagery rescripting, replacement implementation intentions, and imagery rehearsal to target hypothesised mechansims of suicide imagery (Integrated skills for SUicide IMagery; I-SUIM).
Design and Methods: Adult participants with suicide imagery (N = 8) completed two weekly baseline surveys, followed by 3-4 I-SUIM sessions with post-session measures, and a twoweek follow-up survey.

Evaluation included qualitative interviews at follow-up and mixedmethods surveys collecting qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings of suicide imagery duration, coping, imagery meaning, distress, suicide urge, imagery features, and metacognitions.
Results: No participants dropped out of treatment, and there were no series adverse events.
All participants endorsed the intervention as beneficial.
Most reported improved understanding of imagery precipitants and function, meaning, and safety plan use.
Improvements in other mechanisms were more variable, including changes to imagery features, defusion, emotion changes, and metacognitive shifts.
Participants noted some challenges including temporary imagery salience and negative affect immediately following rescripting and difficulty practicing independently.
Participants described the role of an experienced and empathetic therapist important to guide intervention and help them feel less alone.
Limitations: There was no control arm and the study was not designed to demonstrate efficacy.
Conclusions: I-SUIM appears safe and acceptable with qualitatively reported improvements.
However, the specific nature of improvements may vary between individuals, and future research is required to assess efficacy across a range of cognitive, emotional, and behavioural outcomes.
Suicide imagery is a commonly experienced but poorly understood risk factor for suicide.

Mental imagery involves internally experiencing sensory information without corresponding sensory input, including both external (e.g. visual experiences, smell, touch) and internal sensory modalities (e.g., interoception, kinaesthesia) (Kosslyn et al., 2001).

text.text: Imagery about suicide can include mental representations of suicide behaviour sequences ('flash-forwards' imagery; Crane et al., 2012; Hales et al., 2011; Holmes, Crane, et al., 2007), wanted impacts of suicide on the self and others, fantasy-based mental escapes, memories of previous suicide attempts, and even discouraging imagery depicting unwanted impacts of suicide (Crane et al., 2012; Hales et al., 2011; Holmes, Crane, et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2026).

text.text: It is associated with greater risk of both having a detailed suicide plan and having previously enacted suicide behaviours, compared to verbal ideation (Lawrence et al., 2023; Lawrence et al., 2022; Wetherall et al., 2018).

Rahnama and colleagues (2013) treated adults (n = 13) with a history of suicide attempts using two to nine sessions of imagery rescripting based upon Smucker and Dancu's (2005) rescripting protocol for childhood trauma.

text.text: These studies provide preliminary support that imagery rescripting may be useful in the treatment of suicide imagery.

text.text: Thus, suicide imagery may differ from trauma-related imagery in mechanistically important ways, suggesting a need to appropriately tailor interventions.

This study aims to provide a detailed exploration of consumers' phenomenological experiences when engaging in an imagery-based intervention tailored and co-designed for suicide imagery through a mixed-methods case series.
Specifically, the study explores the potential mechanisms of suicide imagery and therapeutic change, as well as consumers' experiences of factors that may facilitate or impede engagement.

This study utilised an exploratory mixed-methods multiple baseline case series design (Yin, 2017) involving a two-week baseline, 3-4 intervention sessions (with pre-and post-session questionnaires), then a follow-up interview and survey 2-weeks post-treatment.

text.text: No primary outcome was specified, as the core aim was to explore potential mechanisms of change that may be suitable for future evaluation.
Data was collected between March and December 2025.

Two Lived Experience Advisors were paid for their time in sharing decision-making regarding study design, materials, and safety protocols via a mixture of written material review and meetings with the lead researcher.
These advisors previously contributed to the development of the intervention.
One advisor (WC) elected to contribute to data analysis and manuscript preparation.
Participants (N = 8) were recruited through online advertisements on social media, newsletters, and via snowball emails.
Adults residing in Australia who experienced suicide imagery in the past month were eligible with referral and safety plan (Stanley & Brown, 2012) from a current therapist.

text.text: After recruiting four participants, the criteria were broadened to allow referral from general practitioners if previous therapy was completed, and for if safety planning was completed at intake.

Exclusion criteria included (1) protective imagery (subjectively perceived to reduce attempt risk) and ( 2) recent (past 3-months) unresolved crisis (e.g., intention, preparation, attempt, crisis support).

text.text: A semi-structured interview guide was developed by AM, PM, FS, and LS and reviewed by two lived experienced advisors (including WC) with recommended changes implemented.

The interview guide assessed recent risk (past-week preparations or intent to suicide), imagery experiences and safety plan use across treatment, and most (and least) helpful intervention components (S1).
Demographics.
A brief questionnaire assessed socio-demographic information at baseline including age, sex, gender, indigeneity, country of birth, and language use.
Items evaluating lifetime history of ideation, plans, and attempts were used to characterise sample suicidality history.

Most items have good test-rest reliability (κ > .69) excepting the ideation item (κ = .39), and all have excellent convergent validity with the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (Posner et al., 2011), (Kappa's > 0.74) (Fox et al., 2020).

text.text: This study piloted initial iterations of the SICS, SIFS, and SIMSscales under development by the study team.
SICS items numerically estimate frequency and duration of suicide imagery and frequency of coping strategy use, and rate interference on a 7-point Likert scale (1= not at all;7 = completely).
The SIFS asks participants to rate pastweek frequency of suicide imagery features (Martin et al., 2026) on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = never;7 = always).

text.text: The SIMS assesses six metacognitive beliefs about suicide imagery on a 7-point scale (1= completely disagree to7= completely agree).
Post-session surveys.
Open-response questions assessed session content, most (and least) helpful aspects, and general feedback.

Therapists also recorded intervention strategies and participant ratings of imagery meaning, coping confidence, distress, and urge to suicide on a scale from0 = not at all, to10 = the strongest ever felt.

Integrated skills for SUicide IMagery (I-SUIM) is a 3-4 session adjunctive intervention that was developed by investigators AM, PM, LS, and FS in collaboration with two lived experience advisors (including WC).
I-SUIM includes the following core components as well as optional formulation-indicated modules.

Intervention begins with assessment and formulation of a target image, then creation of an explicit replacement implementation intention (Adriaanse et al., 2011) outlining typical stressors and coping/safety plan strategies to address needs (e.g., "when I feel isolated, instead of staying on the couch and leaning into my suicide imagery, I will practice my TIP skills, then call my friend Susan.

text.text: If this doesn't work, I will call Lifeline").
Participants' target images and psycho-emotional needs are detailed in Supplementary 2.

Rescripting begins with a stem depicting a typical stressor or 'activating event' for the target image, followed by rescripting including updating of meaning and addressing activated unmet psycho-emotional needs.
This optionally includes positive future imagery.

I-SUIM rescripting then interweaves imaginal rehearsal of the replacement implementation intention (Andersson & Moss, 2011; Divine & Astill, 2025), with motivational emphasis upon imagined benefits (both hedonic and goal-directed) of enacting coping behaviours (Andrade et al., 2025).

The project was conducted in accordance with approved ethics protocols (University of New South Wales Human Research Ethics Committee approval # 7650).
Online surveys were conducted using the REDCap platform, while videoconferencing (Zoom v.6) was used for screening, intervention, and interviews.
Following referral, potential participants completed electronic consent, a brief pre-screening survey, then a screening interview with a clinical researcher (AM or LS).
Enrolled participants completed two weekly baseline surveys before commencing intervention with an experienced clinical psychologist (AM, LS, or GP) who attended fortnightly supervision.
At baseline 1, participants completed demographic and SITBI-SR scales.
The SICS was completed at each baseline and intervention session as well as 2 weeks follow-up.
The SIFS and SIMS were completed at initial baseline 1, session 3, and 2 weeks follow-up.
Interviews were conducted at 2 weeks follow-up by DR, audiorecorded, and transcribed.
Participants were reimbursed for their participation following posttreatment interviews with a $50 e-gift card.

Qualitative interview transcripts then post-session survey data were analysed following six phases of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2021) using NVivo 12 (detailed in S3 alongside reflexivity statements).

text.text: The core analysis team (DR, AM, and WC) utilised audit trails, repeated discussions throughout sense-making, and the application of reflexivity to maintain rigour.
Quantitative data pertaining to demographic information and suicidality history were collated and reported descriptively.

Quantitative ratings of belief in unhelpful meaning, confidence using coping strategies, distress, and suicide urge were summarised descriptively, and effect size (Cohen's d) confidence intervals calculated to provide preliminary effect size estimates for future studies.
Quantitative ratings on the SICS, SIFS, and SIMS were summarised descriptively using medians (due to outlying data points), and individual participant responses plotted.
Eleven potential participants were referred between March and October 2025.
One was excluded due to unresponsiveness to contact attempts, and two were excluded at screening due to lack of past-month imagery.
Eight participants completed intervention sessions between March and December 2025.
Two post-session surveys were not completed after reminder.
One participant was not contactable at follow-up so did not complete the follow-up interview and survey.

text.text: The average age was 43.3 years (SD = 15.9) with average ideation onset at 23.4 years (SD = 14.4), meaning that the average participant had experienced ideation for 19.9 years (SD = 17.1).
All had considered a plan, which onset on average at age 24.1 (SD = 12.9) and which they had considered on 588.1 days across their life on average (SD = 837.2).
Five participants had made an average of four suicide attempts (SD = 2.5), the first of which occurred at age 23.9 on average (SD = 12.7).
One participant had previously completed imagery rescripting unrelated to suicide imagery.
At session 3, Participant 3 reported a lapse in alcohol use attributed to an interpersonal stressor and availability at a party.
At session 4, Participant 4 reported an increase in suiciderelated rehearsal behaviour (not enaction of full suicide plan) attributed to a visitor bringing methods implements into the home.
Local acute mental health services determined the participant did not meet thresholds for imminent risk of harm or require hospitalisation.
Two others described unrelated contextual stressors (Participants 5 and 7):
All eight participants completed all agreed sessions of the intervention (n =6 completed 4 sessions, n = 2 completed 3) and targeted one image (n = 4 over 2 rescripts, n = 4 over 3 rescripts).
Supplementary File 2 details participants' target imagery, meaning, and included I-SUIM strategies.
Participants were moderately confident that session content would help (M = 4.79; SD = 1.26).
Almost all sessions were rated as being the perfect pace (n = 25), while 3 sessions were rated as too rushed.
Almost all (27/28) sessions were rated as mostly to completely understood.

Thematic analysis resulted in four themes pertaining to experiences of change and two themes describing experiences of engaging with the intervention process (themes and associated codes outlined in Table 2).

text.text: Most participants reported increased understanding of factors contributing to the onset and maintenance of their suicide imagery.
Participants spoke of a deepened or newfound understanding of precipitants, including situational events and internal emotional states.
While in some cases this made the images clearer, this also helped participants understand how they could mitigate precipitants or respond in other, healthier ways.
"And so there's a point in time, just before that habit kicks in, and I can, we identified that I can make a choice.
And so it's helpful in terms of identifying that pattern" -Participant 2

Participants also reported increased understanding of the function of their suicide imagery: "We were able to work out a little bit about maybe what drives it …having an understanding about what it might actually be providing me, … was interesting … [and] helpful"-Participant 4 "[The suicide imagery is] something that I'm doing just as a coping mechanism …making sure I have escape routes … a way to just jump out when things get too hard.
Now I'm aware that I'm doing that." -Participant 8
Participants reported improvements in their experiences of suicide imagery.
This included changes to imagery content, frequency, meaning, metacognitions, and psychological distancing.

Some imagery content changes including coping and less lethality: "[The imagery] is just less destructive … normally, if you're having imagery, its like …you're reliving a moment of like … you're thinking of what's going to happen in the future … if [you attempt suicide].

[Now the imagery] has slowed down and … you just don't follow through." -Participant 6 "[I] leant into the rescripted image and so I guess … It did change, because it became something else" -Participant 8
Others reported that it has changed to include connection to the unwanted impacts on others, which was a desired inclusion to motivate them to stay alive.
"I have that connection [now].
text.formatted: "I have that connection <ref type="bibr">[now]</ref>.

text.text: And I'm really pleased as a result.

Like, it doesn't make me feel good, but it's a connection that I want to have…I felt that they [those strategies] helped…." -Participant 5 "I do less planning … I don't fully plan if I actually want to suicide or not.
It's more of a like, 'I could've done that, but like I shouldn't have'.

I just think that it could impact others around me." -Participant 6 Two participants reported that the content of their imagery did not shift: "They haven't changed for me, probably, because they're so ingrained, compared to, like, four rescripting sessions." -Participant 4 Some participants reported a notable decrease in frequency and intrusiveness, which some attributed to deliberate use of strategies to pre-emptively meet their needs.

Other participants reported no change in frequency, noting continued stressors: "it's more external triggers that are setting me off, so it's… It hasn't really changed the frequency." -Participant 8 "It depends on the situation.
So, yeah, the last fortnight, there's been a few triggers that have brought it on, whereas the fortnight before there might not have been any.

Some participants reported that the meaning of their specific suicide imagery did not change ("not really, it's quite the same" -Participant 6), while others did report a shift in meaning: "I can have contact/brush past my old suicidal thoughts but this time I feel I have more control over them and that doesn't represent an inevitability [anymore]" -Participant 5
Most participants reported a shift in their relationship to their suicide imagery.
This included greater psychological distancing or cognitive defusion from their imagery: "It felt like it was just part of me before.

Now it feels like it might be a little bit separate." -Participant 1 "My concern was that they would push me over the edge … I can think about it and dismiss it now … they mean less … they don't own me".
Most participants reported improved emotional impact of their suicide imagery.
This included increased positive affect, reduced negative affect, and for some included reduced suicide urges.
Participants described a variety of positive emotions, including hope, empowerment, and.
self-compassion: "It's given me a bit more confidence to not be afraid … It was empowering…" -Participant 5 "That self-compassion … the self-awareness and inner growth.
It's revolutionised things.
… I'm down another road.
Optimistic.
Positive.
Empowered." -Participant 7.
Most participants reported decreased negative emotions.

Several reported improved perceptions and use of their safety plan: "I think I was just more inclined to use it after the imagery practice" -Participant 4 "I definitely use it more.

Even during the day, or just when I'm really stressed out." -Participant 6, "I use it more because I was practicing … it's sitting a tiny bit better, now that it's attached to a skill" -Participant 1 "certain steps in my safety plan that we've added to the rescript … made it helpful … grounding and box breathing that…changed everything" -Participant 8 Some participants noted that their suicide imagery is much shorter in duration because they are now able to intervene earlier before they become overly distressed "It only lasts seconds, really, because I immediately clamp it down" -Participant 7 "I'm able to just also use the methods…before it…progresses into something more aggressive and more…hard to control…" -Participant 6 However, one participant noted that this was less effective during instances of stronger distress:
Some participants reported challenges to engaging in the intervention including discomfort and difficulty practicing independently.
Some also reported transient increases to imagery salience following rescripting.
A couple of participants reported finding the first session to be uncomfortable and intimidating ("a bit uncomfortable at the beginning" -Participant 4).
Some described difficulty engaging when rescripting involved fantastical (non-realistic) or more emotionally intense content.

"When I tried to turn major issues into a smaller picture, or pause them, and it wouldn't work from a visualisation perspective." -Participant 5 Some participants reported that the imagery rehearsal was challenging to do independently, either due to difficulty with mind-wandering rumination or difficulty believing the imagery when self-directed.

"It was very challenging to do it independently…The suicidal imagery would then take over from that re-scripting when doing independent practice" -Participant 4 "I find it easier when someone leads me through it.
I don't like to do it myself.
I'm naturally resistant to going, 'oh, I'm so awesome, I'm great at my job.'
But when someone [is] running it … and let them guide me.
That way I was able to imagine all of the things and I think to unlock that potential" -Participant 5
When queried, four participants (1, 2, 6, and 8) described a short-term increase in their suicide imagery, which one likened to a hangover.
Participants reported that this was generally quite minor and manageable.
"That had a short term, half day negative impact on me, which, which is fine.
Certainly manageable" -Participant 2 "A bit, but …it goes away.
After a couple hours … It's still fresh in your mind." -Participant 6

When explicitly queried, one participant did note a temporary increase in their inclination to suicide during this period, but which they did not act upon and were able to respond to using the coping and safety strategies.
For most this impact lasted a few hours, but one participant reported that it lasted up to a day or two.
Most participants reported that they would have liked more sessions to allow them to engage with the intervention more deeply and allow them to consolidate their new skills.
Others reported that four sessions was an adequate treatment length, but suggested that session number could be adjusted to meet individual needs.
A couple of participants reported that they found the 90-minute sessions a little too long, but most reported that the duration was important to allow adequate time to engage with the treatment.
"I found it really hard to get through it.
But at the same time, … if you'd have any less time…you wouldn't have time to do what was needed" -Participant 5
Participants also described therapist factors which facilitated their engagement.
These included having expert guidance, emotional support, and validation while discussing imagery, often for the first time.
Participants noted that having a therapist who was emotionally supportive allowed them to engage, feel validated, and less alone.
and make sense and to not pay too much attention to it." -Participant 4 "It is hard to deal with suicidal thoughts and images alone.

It has been nice to be able to talk about it without making everyone feel uncomfortable" -Participant 8 Some participants commented that this was their first experience discussing their suicide imagery, either at all or in detail.
Participants mentioned that they felt shame or were afraid to explore their images more for fear it would make them more potent.
Others reported reluctance from their usual mental healthcare providers to discuss their suicide imagery.

"it was the first rock solid, deep conversation about it, which isn't easy but it's the conversation itself was really useful …" -Participant 2 These conversations appeared to reduce shame and did not result in the participants' expected increase or progression of the suicidal thoughts.

One participant noted that while this wasn't the first time she discussed the images, going through that process with a therapist who was calm and didn't over-react was a positive aspect of the intervention.

Some participants reported that the presence of an experienced therapist to guide the intervention was crucial to facilitate their understanding and reduce apprehension. "[therapist]'s targeted questions, facilitated a clarity there. … having someone there to guide me and keep me safe while I was playing in that space, and that meant that I wasn't concerned as much as I would be in the absence of someone who knows what they're doing, guiding me" -Participant 5Quantitative Ratings

text.text: Visual inspection suggests that weekly imagery duration decreased over treatment for around half of participants, without change in interference ratings.
Note that participants 4 and 7 reported substantial increases to known imagery triggers at session 4 and follow-up respectively, which corresponded with increased duration at these timepoints.

Note also that in session 3, participant 5 elected to deliberately evoke additional imagery of the unwanted impacts of suicide on their family as a deterrent to suicide, which was followed by increased duration in session 4 and follow-up.
There were overall low frequencies of suicide crisis requiring safety plan use, leading to floor effects (S4).

These suggest medium to very large reductions in the strength of the unhelpful meaning of target imagery, and small to very large increases in participant confidence implementing the coping strategies from their safety plans.
The effect size confidence intervals were wide due to the small sample, so point estimates need to be interpreted with caution.

text.text: Seven participants displayed reductions in unhelpful meaning over time.
Four demonstrated a partial return in meaning strength during the period between rescripting sessions, but these tended to reduce following repeated rescripting.
Most participants demonstrated modest increases in coping confidence and decreases in distress.
Although two participants demonstrated decreases in suicide urge over sessions, for most this remained stable and low (around 0-2/10 urge).

Within individual sessions, ratings of both distress and suicide urge often increased between pre-rescript (prior to any experiential work) and mid-rescripting (after evocation of their distressing 'stem' image), before decreasing post-rescripting.

About half the sample showed reductions in the frequency of imagery with feasible methods, detail, being dead, enacting methods, suicide behaviour but including barriers, and negative impacts on the self.

Baseline intrusivity was high but reduced for about half of participants.
Baseline endorsement of imagery risk was low to moderate, but increased for about a third of participants.
Disengage difficulty appeared to reduce for the third of participants with initially high ratings.

This mixed-methods case series explored consumer experiences of a tailored intervention for suicide imagery, with the primary aim to identify potential mechanisms of change for evaluation in future research.

The study expanded previous research (Rahnama et al., 2013; Schmaal et al., 2026) by identifying a broad range of potential mechanisms of therapeutic change among a sample of adults with relatively severe and longstanding suicidality.
text.formatted: The study expanded previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rahnama et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Schmaal et al., 2026)</ref> by identifying a broad range of potential mechanisms of therapeutic change among a sample of adults with relatively severe and longstanding suicidality.

text.text: Few constructs demonstrated reliable improvement across participants.
However, all participants reported improvements on at least one construct, and all endorsed the intervention as beneficial.
The study also identified several process considerations for facilitating engagement.
Almost all participants reported improved understanding of imagery precipitants and function and perceived control.

Consistent with hypothesised mechanisms of imagery rescripting (Arntz, 2012), I-SUIM was associated with average reductions in unhelpful imagery meanings, estimated to be of at least moderate to very large effects.
text.formatted: Consistent with hypothesised mechanisms of imagery rescripting <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Arntz, 2012)</ref>, I-SUIM was associated with average reductions in unhelpful imagery meanings, estimated to be of at least moderate to very large effects.

text.text: Consistent with the use of implementation intention (Andersson & Moss, 2011) and imagery rehearsal strategies (Andrade et al., 2025), almost all participants qualitatively reported increases in safety plan strategy use.
text.formatted: Consistent with the use of implementation intention <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andersson & Moss, 2011)</ref> and imagery rehearsal strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Andrade et al., 2025)</ref>, almost all participants qualitatively reported increases in safety plan strategy use.

text.text: Average improvement in coping confidence was estimated to be at least small to a very large effect.
Although quantitative estimates of safety plan strategy use were stably low, this item was anchored to infrequent crisis contexts.
In contrast, qualitative data suggested increases in safety plan strategy use earlier in trajectories to pre-empt crisis.
Future studies might explore therapeutic change across insight and positive coping strategies more broadly beyond worst-point crisis.
There was variability in the specific aspects of imagery that demonstrated change.

Around half reported change to concrete imagery features (e.g., less lethal methods depictions) while others reported improved psychological distancing from their imagery or metacognitive shifts (e.g., increased sense of control).
Changes to emotional responses similarly varied to include reduced negative emotions (e.g., distress) for some and improved positive emotions (e.g., self-compassion, empowerment) for others.
Therapeutic improvements may therefore manifest idiosyncratically, cautioning against the use of limited universal outcome metrics.
Future studies may instead consider classifying participants as responders based on improvement on any among a range of outcomes.
Only half of participants demonstrated reductions in imagery duration, with a few demonstrating increases alongside increases in external stressors.
This aligns with broader research demonstrating that fluctuates in response to contextual drivers such as housing, finances, and workplace stressors (Gallagher et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This aligns with broader research demonstrating that fluctuates in response to contextual drivers such as housing, finances, and workplace stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gallagher et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies may consider tracking fluctuations in contextual stressors alongside clinical outcomes.
The study also aimed to explore consumer experiences of engaging with the intervention process.

Engagement was high, with all participants completing all planned intervention sessions despite increased contextual stressors for some, compared to drop-out rates between 10-14% for other brief interventions (Andreasson et al., 2016; Comtois et al., 2011) and 24-48% for longer interventions (Linehan et al., 2015).

text.text: This suggests that the intervention was acceptable and engaging to participants, despite the relative severity of the sample.

Some challenges were identified including activation of difficult emotions and transient increases in imagery salience following rescripting, which once participant acknowledged was associated with processing previously avoided stressors and suicide imagery in treatment.

Studies of imagery-related interventions for trauma reliably report that small subsets of participants may experience transient increases in distress and trauma symptoms that are not associated with poor outcomes or drop-out (Burger et al., 2023; Kullberg et al., 2025; Larsen et al., 2016).

text.text: It is also important to note that imagery rescripting requires deliberate activation of 'hotspots' of difficult images and emotion for optimal treatment response (Arntz, 2025).
text.formatted: It is also important to note that imagery rescripting requires deliberate activation of 'hotspots' of difficult images and emotion for optimal treatment response <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Arntz, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, the participants (1, 2, 6, and 8) who endorsed this transient increase were among those with larger reductions in suicide image duration, unhelpful meaning, overall distress, and suicide urge.

Although these transient symptom increases may be expected among a subset of participants and are not indicative of poor outcomes, it is nonetheless important that clinicians discuss this possibility during informed consent.
Participants also described therapist-related factors important for engagement, including the need for an experienced therapist to guide the intervention and provide emotional validation.
Participants also noted the value of discussing their imagery with a trained therapist, often for the first time.
These findings suggest that careful work may be required to translate the I-SUIM intervention to non-contiguous intervention formats such as online modules.
Limitations inherent to the study's design include lack of control arm, small sample unpowered for inferential evaluation of efficacy, and no post-treatment evaluation of suicide behaviours.
Full-powered randomised controlled efficacy trials are required to draw conclusions regarding treatment impact.
Further, this sample experienced chronic suicidality, with an average duration approaching 20 years.
It is unclear how the intervention may be experienced by individuals with more recently onset suicide imagery.
Measures used to evaluate suicide imagery duration and safety plan strategy use were also limited.
Although sessions targeted only a single suicide image, items assessing imagery duration enquired regarding suicide imagery in general (most reported a range of imagery on intake).
If intervention effects did not generalise to non-targeted suicide imagery, these benefits may have been obscured in broad outcome data.
Conversely, participants often presented with narrow safety plans which were elaborated on during treatment to include a broader range of coping strategies.
However, items assessing safety plan use were anchored to crisis points where the specific safety plan was used.
Thus, quantitative estimates may not have captured instances where broader coping strategies were used, or strategies applied prior to crisis.
Future studies may consider evaluating change in targeted imagery, as well as implementation of broader coping strategies prior to suicide crisis.

This study provides preliminary support that I-SUIM provides a safe and acceptable brief intervention for suicide imagery among adults with chronic suicidality, with qualitatively reported improvements for all participants.

The nature of treatment improvements may be variable between individuals, and further research is required to evaluate treatment efficacy and the impact of I-SUIM upon a range of cognitive, emotional, and behavioural outcomes.

"[I-SUIM]…reduced the hopelessness and anxiety …Immediately during the intervention there was improvements to my imagery.

But having that carry across for, like, a week, to, like, now this is two weeks post, it hasn't quite carried across for me, but that may be due to my difficulties in practicing [the rescripting] independently." -Participant 4 "I've had a lot of pressure in the last few weeks, because I've returned to work properly, and you know what?

I'm not depressed, I'm not anxious, and I'm not suicidal, so my life is stable and doable, achievable, and I've been able to maintain.". -Participant 5 A few reported reduced suicide urges: "also just less … wanting to kill myself" -Participant 6 "It's reduced my urges." -Participant 5 "I feel quite resolute … not doing that [suicide]" -Participant 7 Change Theme 4: More Adaptive Behavioural Responses Most participants reported changes in their behavioural responses to suicide imagery.
These included the use of new imagery-based strategies, increased safety plan engagement, and intervention earlier in suicide imagery trajectories before crisis point.
Some participants reported benefitting from the foundational realisation that they can use imagery-based strategies, not just verbal strategies.

"I feel like you've given me access to a toolbox…You don't just have to control things with tablets and words, you can also do it with images" -Participant 5 Some highlighted the benefit of being able to manipulate their imagery or deliberately evoke positive or corrective imagery to challenge suicide imagery appraisals: "It's given me the option of 'hang on.

You're not going to get me because I've got this tool here that I can…challenge you with it." -Participant 1 "…being able to call upon positive memories…when they [suicide images] do come up, you're better able to switch them…" -Participant 6 Two participants utilised recordings (made upon request) to challenge their imagery: "So, now, I try to roll through the script, and I have got it recorded on my phone so I can listen to it.
So, I can try to change the progression of my thoughts.
